		<title>Five Signals From The 2026 Functional Verification Study</title>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Functional verification is no longer only about closing the design. It is increasingly about understanding the system before silicon becomes the first place where all interactions are fully revealed.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/five-signals-from-the-2026-functional-verification-study/">Five Signals From The 2026 Functional Verification Study</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The forthcoming 2026 Siemens EDA and Wilson Research Group Functional Verification Study indicates that the IC verification problem is changing in nature, not simply growing in complexity. Declining first-silicon success, increased CPU/GPU/AI accelerator-class participation, near-universal reported embedded processor content across implementation categories, a broadening verification ecosystem, and greater visibility of firmware-, safety-, and security-related respin contributors all point toward a shift from verifying designs to building system confidence in software-driven silicon systems.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" fetchpriority="high" decoding="async" class="alignnone wp-image-24281784" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-21-at-12.49.40-PM.png?resize=554%2C292&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="554" height="292" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-21-at-12.49.40-PM.png?resize=300%2C158&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-21-at-12.49.40-PM.png?resize=1024%2C539&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-21-at-12.49.40-PM.png?resize=768%2C405&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-21-at-12.49.40-PM.png?resize=600%2C316&amp;ssl=1 600w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-21-at-12.49.40-PM.png?w=1420&amp;ssl=1 1420w" sizes="(max-width: 554px) 100vw, 554px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig.1: First-silicon success trend, showing the long historical equilibrium followed by a recent decline. Source: Siemens EDA</strong></p>
<p>Read <a href="https://resources.sw.siemens.com/en-US/white-paper-five-signals-from-the-2026-functional-verification-study/">more here.</a></p>

		<title>Build Secure SoCs From The Start</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/build-secure-socs-from-the-start/</link>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Practical guide to hardware security assurance in modern semiconductor design.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/build-secure-socs-from-the-start/">Build Secure SoCs From The Start</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<div class="dl-intro">
<p>Modern semiconductor systems have reached unprecedented levels of complexity.</p>
<p>Today’s system-on-chip (SoC) architectures integrate hundreds of heterogeneous IP blocks, multiple compute engines, shared memory hierarchies, and extensive firmware and software stacks.</p>
<p>While these capabilities enable powerful computing platforms, including AI and machine learning, they also expand the hardware attack surface deep into the silicon architecture.</p>
<p>With this eBook, you will learn how to:</p>
</div>
<div class="dl-bullets">
<ul>
<li>Detect vulnerabilities early in the development lifecycle.</li>
<li>Reduce costly silicon respins.</li>
<li>Deliver secure silicon products with greater confidence.</li>
</ul>
</div>
<p>Read <a href="https://explore.arteris.com/ebook-build-secure-socs-from-the-start">more here</a>.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/build-secure-socs-from-the-start/">Build Secure SoCs From The Start</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>

		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Liz Allan]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Wed, 23 Sep 2026 07:01:47 +0000</pubDate>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>A mixture of expert agentic AI systems can focus on their tasks with or without a commanding general, but challenges remain in drawing boundaries between human and AI effort. </p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/multi-agent-ai-systems-must-work-like-an-orchestra-without-a-conductor/">Multi-Agent AI Systems Must Work Like An Orchestra Without A Conductor</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p><b><span data-contrast="none">Key Takeaways:</span></b><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<ul>
<li aria-setsize="-1" data-leveltext="" data-font="Symbol" data-listid="1" data-list-defn-props="{&quot;335552541&quot;:1,&quot;335559685&quot;:720,&quot;335559991&quot;:360,&quot;469769226&quot;:&quot;Symbol&quot;,&quot;469769242&quot;:[8226],&quot;469777803&quot;:&quot;left&quot;,&quot;469777804&quot;:&quot;&quot;,&quot;469777815&quot;:&quot;hybridMultilevel&quot;}" data-aria-posinset="1" data-aria-level="1"><span data-contrast="none">Multi-agentic systems have evolved into a dynamic, task-based organization of skills with a flatter hierarchy than a traditional military force, and some are headless.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></li>
<li aria-setsize="-1" data-leveltext="" data-font="Symbol" data-listid="1" data-list-defn-props="{&quot;335552541&quot;:1,&quot;335559685&quot;:720,&quot;335559991&quot;:360,&quot;469769226&quot;:&quot;Symbol&quot;,&quot;469769242&quot;:[8226],&quot;469777803&quot;:&quot;left&quot;,&quot;469777804&quot;:&quot;&quot;,&quot;469777815&quot;:&quot;hybridMultilevel&quot;}" data-aria-posinset="2" data-aria-level="1"><span data-contrast="none">Agentic capabilities will also come from physical, deterministic engines, and those agents will talk to other agents in different formats to help ensure 100% accuracy, which AI models alone cannot achieve.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></li>
<li aria-setsize="-1" data-leveltext="" data-font="Symbol" data-listid="1" data-list-defn-props="{&quot;335552541&quot;:1,&quot;335559685&quot;:720,&quot;335559991&quot;:360,&quot;469769226&quot;:&quot;Symbol&quot;,&quot;469769242&quot;:[8226],&quot;469777803&quot;:&quot;left&quot;,&quot;469777804&quot;:&quot;&quot;,&quot;469777815&quot;:&quot;hybridMultilevel&quot;}" data-aria-posinset="3" data-aria-level="1"><span data-contrast="none">Human effort is needed to ensure a design can be copyrightable, and on-prem proprietary models are another way to ensure prompt IQ and IP are not lost.</span></li>
</ul>
<hr />
<p><b><span data-contrast="none">Experts At The Table</span></b><span data-contrast="none"><strong>:</strong> Semiconductor Engineering sat down to discuss recent developments and challenges when using agentic AI for chip design, with Matt Graham, senior group director of verification software product management at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/cadence-design-systems/" data-uw-rm-brl="PR" data-uw-original-href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/cadence-design-systems/">Cadence</a>; Harrison Balistreri, head of business development and strategic partnerships at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/alpha-design-ai-chipagents/" data-uw-rm-brl="PR" data-uw-original-href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/alpha-design-ai-chipagents/">ChipAgents</a>; Alexander Petr, senior director and portfolio manager at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/keysight-technologies/" data-uw-rm-brl="PR" data-uw-original-href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/keysight-technologies/">Keysight EDA</a>; Sathish Balasubramanian, head of product for EDA AI at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/mentor-a-siemens-business/" data-uw-rm-brl="PR" data-uw-original-href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/mentor-a-siemens-business/">Siemens EDA</a>; and Anand Thiruvengadam, executive director and head of AI product management at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/synopsys-inc/" data-uw-rm-brl="PR" data-uw-original-href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/synopsys-inc/">Synopsys</a>. This roundtable was held behind closed doors at the recent Design Automation Conference. What follows are excerpts of that discussion.</span><span data-contrast="none"> This is the third part of a three-part series. Part one is </span><a href="https://semiengineering.com/agentic-ai-success-relies-on-excellent-human-scaffolding/"><span data-contrast="none">here</span></a><span data-contrast="none">. Part two is <a href="https://semiengineering.com/token-costs-are-becoming-the-new-eda-budget-battle/">here</a>.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-large wp-image-24280545" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Image-from-iOS-10.gif?resize=1024%2C299&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1024" height="299" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Image-from-iOS-10.gif?resize=1024%2C299&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Image-from-iOS-10.gif?resize=300%2C88&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Image-from-iOS-10.gif?resize=768%2C224&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Image-from-iOS-10.gif?resize=600%2C175&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p><b><span data-contrast="none">L-R: Synopsys’ Thiruvengadam; Keysight’s Petr; Cadence’s Graham; ChipAgents’ Balistreri; and Siemens’ Balasubramanian.</span></b><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><b><span data-contrast="auto">SE:  Many agentic flows involve a mixture of experts (MoE) or a hierarchy of multi-agents with some type of leader at the top. What developments are you seeing there? Is it a top-down, military-style organization with various security and access clearances, or more of a horizontal team?</span></b><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><b><span data-contrast="auto">Graham: </span></b><span data-contrast="auto">It is becoming much flatter than an army. If you&#8217;d asked me a year ago, I might have said, yes, it is a big hierarchy of agents. There will be mini agents, sub agents, and low agents. There will be generals and lieutenants and whatever else, all the way up. But AI in general, not just EDA, we are migrating much more toward a flat set of skills, or capabilities, or features, or knowledge, or whatever the word is you want to use to describe it. Everything is overloaded with terms. What we&#8217;re seeing becomes a much more dynamic, task-based organization of skills into almost dynamic agents. There is one general, if you like, or commander.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><b><span data-contrast="auto">Balasubramanian: </span></b><span data-contrast="auto">Orchestrator.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><b><span data-contrast="auto">Graham: </span></b><span data-contrast="auto">Right. And everything else below tends to be much flatter. I can pick and choose quickly to assemble my troops, but it’s much less like an army with a mechanized division and an airborne division, or something else. We have troops. Those troops have skills, and we assemble the right troops for the task dynamically, because we&#8217;re not bound, as armies are, by logistical and physical reality.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><b><span data-contrast="auto">Petr: </span></b><span data-contrast="auto">You’re better off comparing it to an orchestra. You have one conductor, and you have groups who play certain instruments. They can play individually, or they can play together. They can also play synchronously or asynchronously to achieve certain tunes and then play together.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><b><span data-contrast="auto">Balasubramanian: </span></b><span data-contrast="auto">That&#8217;s very important. Even if it&#8217;s flat, the key thing is that everyone knows their part, and they also know how they connect to everyone else. Everyone knows the end goal. Nothing is siloed. They all play by the same tune. If you look at a symphony orchestra, everyone knows everyone else. They can read the notes. They know what to do, what not to do, how to do it. </span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><b><span data-contrast="auto">Petr: </span></b><span data-contrast="auto">There are borders, guardrails. They all ground it.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><b><span data-contrast="auto">Balasubramanian: </span></b><span data-contrast="auto">The term I see quite a bit is headless agents. There&#8217;s no concept of having a big master agent doing everything else. We call it a headless way of working, and it&#8217;s been quite popular on the software side. It&#8217;s coming here, and what I see going forward is customers are interacting with tools. They won&#8217;t even know what the tool is. From our side, we are going to build agentic capabilities coming out of the physical engines, or deterministic engines around those engines, and that&#8217;s going to be an agent on its own. It can talk to other agents. It can understand different formats and where it sits. It can talk to understand design. Designers can interact with it, make it do work. That&#8217;s where the future is going.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><b><span data-contrast="auto">Thiruvengadam: </span></b><span data-contrast="auto">What Matt said is very interesting. We are essentially making the point that you should be thinking about digital organization—human organization, human hierarchy, digital hierarchy, roughly speaking —which is correct. But also, the fluidity of that is very important. It won&#8217;t be a rigid, hard structure. Ebb and flow will happen. It can change, depending on the complexity of the commands. The fluidity is very important. You will have a layer that orchestrates and calls upon ‘resources’ as needed to execute. This is very important. At some point in the future, it might graduate to something where it&#8217;s maybe autonomous. That is about abstraction again. We are talking about taking layer after layer of abstraction away, one by one, but we&#8217;re not there yet.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><b><span data-contrast="auto">Balistreri: </span></b><span data-contrast="auto">We have products where agents propose hypotheses and do tournament-style ranking. We have a judging agent, but there&#8217;s a lot of nuance in this idea of agents, where you could throw many agents at the problem. But if they all come up with similar hypotheses for the problem, it doesn&#8217;t matter how many agents you deploy or how good your judging agent is. It has a lot to do with how you manage context, and it comes back to local versus global context. It doesn&#8217;t matter how you deploy agents if they all have the same local context. To get the benefit of deploying agents at scale, you need to manage which hypotheses each agent generates and where that context comes from. To do that, you also can&#8217;t have point agents. You can&#8217;t do point acceleration around one tool. Agents become powerful when they can deliver the full flow. The full flow requires encoding in your agent loops how to view some of this context and how to manage that, so that you get the benefit of many parallel agents instead of them just trying to converge on the same thing.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><b><span data-contrast="auto">Graham: </span></b><span data-contrast="auto">There are two sides to that, and I agree for the most part. But I&#8217;ll draw a parallel to how synthesis changed electronic design. The vast majority of gates built now are synthesized gates. The agent writes RTL. Then, RTL gets synthesized. But there is still a certain percentage, depending on the application, that must be either hand-synthesized or laid out by hand. There will still be significant opportunity to accelerate the tools. I wouldn&#8217;t call it a point agent necessarily. But in agentifying the tool for a specific task, a smaller percentage will still need to be hand-coded, in the same way that we still hand-assemble some instructions for a PC or for any compute platform. Expecting 100% autonomy is setting too high a bar that I don&#8217;t know we can achieve. I don&#8217;t think it&#8217;s realistic or even worthwhile. Setting it at 99-point-some-odd-nines  still leaves a huge amount of work to be done, and accelerating the tools themselves is still important, but I agree that it&#8217;s not the bulk of the time. </span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><b><span data-contrast="auto">Balistreri: </span></b><span data-contrast="auto">This might be an unpopular opinion in this room, but we can talk about accelerating existing tools, or we can talk about new tools entirely. When we talk to our customers, one of the biggest bottlenecks in taping out their chips is that they don&#8217;t have enough on-premises compute to run existing EDA tools. Can you rearchitect tools to be optimized for agent use, speed up runtime, and run more tools in parallel? Then there&#8217;s the other question of, &#8216;Do the models subsume it?&#8217; In some of the complex tasks that are still hand-placed, there is an opportunity for models to take that on and solve extremely complex problems that humans just couldn&#8217;t hold in their heads. Think about all those tables you had to look at on the wall. Back in the day, you were laying sheets across a giant table to look at the resistance and capacitance and placing them for analog. All of that, I think, can be captured inside of models. </span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><b><span data-contrast="auto">Graham: </span></b><span data-contrast="auto">It can be. The question is, how soon will it be efficient? We&#8217;ve spent a huge amount of time solving that problem deterministically, algorithmically, and mathematically so that we get the right answer every single time. What you&#8217;re proposing is, &#8216;Can we use a probabilistic model to solve those problems more efficiently?&#8217; Today, &#8216;no&#8217; is the very clear answer. With the speed of technological advancement, will that be compute-efficient and dollar-efficient in the next 2 years, 8 years, 10 years? </span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><b><span data-contrast="auto">Thiruvengadam: </span></b><span data-contrast="auto">I agree. The key point, again, is the march of nines. The march of nines will kick in, and you&#8217;ve got a 99.99999. You need to get 100% accuracy. We&#8217;re talking about subsuming two EDA tools into models. </span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><b><span data-contrast="auto">Balasubramanian: </span></b><span data-contrast="auto">That&#8217;s very important. In chip design, being 99.99% accurate is a failure. All it takes is one picosecond and you have a whole violation. </span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><b><span data-contrast="auto">Petr: </span></b><span data-contrast="auto">We keep forgetting that we still have not fully understood all the physics. Every single model we have is a simplification of the real world. It&#8217;s an error of an error of an error of an error. No matter how well you go on the whole agentic framework, at some point, there&#8217;s a trade-off somewhere. And if you don&#8217;t capture that, your chip is dead. We spent decades optimizing the simulator engines to get deterministic results. There&#8217;s always an argument in those AI frameworks, ‘Oh, just run reinforcement learning. It can do it.’ Fair, it can. But my mathematically based optimizer is still faster and more accurate. Why would I want to do that?</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><b><span data-contrast="auto">Thiruvengadam: </span></b><span data-contrast="auto">It&#8217;s important to understand that the march of nines is a problem in software. Why would it not be a problem in hardware? In chip design, it&#8217;s even more of a problem. In software, they talk about getting 100%. Failure is an important part. In hardware, costs are so high that the march of nines becomes an even bigger problem. </span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><b><span data-contrast="auto">Balasubramanian: </span></b><span data-contrast="auto">As we go down the flow, the band of how much error you can tolerate drops drastically.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><b><span data-contrast="auto">SE: In an orchestral multi-agentic flow, who has a kill switch to prevent agents from burning through tokens and trying forever to gain 100% coverage closure, for example?</span></b><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><b><span data-contrast="auto">Graham: </span></b><span data-contrast="auto">This is part of the prep before you deploy, which must be part of the infrastructure. We all have infrastructure this must sit on — the guardrails. There are still infinite problems in IC design and verification. Fundamentally, it&#8217;s an infinite or near-infinite problem, so there must be guardrails somewhere on how much time, how many tokens, and what the tool covers, etc. One thing EDA has been good at over the years is having tool providers address that with customers, having customers understand the best ROI trade-offs, and pushing us to provide them. Up until now, it was cycles on a given problem. We get the number of CPU cycles we think we need to do, whether we get them in the cloud or on-prem or whatever, for one of the thousand tasks you have to do from RTL to GDS. Now we&#8217;re adding tokens to those, but we need the same guardrails. We know this. Our customers employ entire departments of people to optimize this exact problem.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><b><span data-contrast="auto">Petr: </span></b><span data-contrast="auto">Infinite loops are not new to us. Every mathematical problem has infinite loops. If you get into those trenches, we have solutions.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><b><span data-contrast="auto">SE: What about IP ownership if you&#8217;re using an agent for a design that you sell to a customer, or they use your agent for their design, who owns what IP?</span></b><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><b><span data-contrast="auto">Balasubramanian: </span></b><span data-contrast="auto">IP ownership is one of the biggest concerns I&#8217;m hearing about, both from our side as the tool provider and from the customer side. Yes, [agents] can write code, but the challenge is that all it takes is one copyrighted piece of code getting into your codebase, and if you don&#8217;t verify it, you&#8217;re going to get a loss. That&#8217;s one thing. Second, the most important thing is, I always tell people that any prompt you do, that&#8217;s your IQ. You&#8217;re doing your foundation, you&#8217;re using Claude Code, and you&#8217;re letting your designers do certain things. Their prompt will be, ‘This is how I&#8217;m going to be solving this routing problem. Can you do this?’ Your prompt is pretty much your IP. You&#8217;re telling some people the algorithm for how to do certain things, and there is a lot of talk about, ‘They&#8217;re not going to look at it.’ But every prompt is necessary to the LLM providers. If it goes outside of the air gap, it&#8217;s a problem. So IP protection is going to be very key. How do you expose code outside, especially source code? That&#8217;s going to be very key, and that&#8217;s a big concern coming up.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><b><span data-contrast="auto">Petr: </span></b><span data-contrast="auto">Another problem is that U.S. copyright does not allow us to copyright code that has been generated by an AI. That means every chip designed by an AI isn&#8217;t copyrightable.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><b><span data-contrast="auto">Balasubramanian: </span></b><span data-contrast="auto">Yes, because LLMs are not [copyrightable].</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><b><span data-contrast="auto">Thiruvengadam: </span></b><span data-contrast="auto">The key distinction is that we are not talking about a chip that&#8217;s 100% designed by AI with no human intervention.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><b><span data-contrast="auto">Petr: </span></b><span data-contrast="auto">There&#8217;s a clause in the copyright that says the majority of the [design] has to be done by a human and, I’m sorry to say that, but the majority is not going to be. </span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><b><span data-contrast="auto">Balistreri: </span></b><span data-contrast="auto">I want to recap a bit and then get to this point. There are many problems, many layers of problems, with deploying AI in a high ROI way that organizations will accept meets their security requirements. One is cost. We solve that at the harness layer. The same model, doing like-for-like tasks, uses 40% fewer tokens. Our own model is open-weight and performs similarly, but at lower cost. Then there&#8217;s the full-flow problem, which is where you need the ontology. You can&#8217;t just do point acceleration. Then there&#8217;s the autonomous problem, which is the trust. Are there going to be critical errors? Are those gated and built into your system so you can&#8217;t produce things? Then there&#8217;s the IP and security issue, and it&#8217;s a pretty simple question. Do you want to send your inference over the public internet to a model provider that is building chips that compete with your chips? If you use frontier models in your agentic layer, whatever agents you use, you run that risk. Some don&#8217;t even have zero data retention. The clear answer to us — in a highly security-focused industry, where your design and design flow itself is IP — is that you need a solution with a custom model you can deploy on-prem. That also solves the IP question. I&#8217;m not a copyright lawyer, but if the design never leaves your environment, it&#8217;s de facto still yours. It&#8217;s not copyrighted per se, but no one else can access it. </span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<p><b><span data-contrast="auto">Petr: </span></b><span data-contrast="auto">Don&#8217;t underestimate reverse engineering.</span><span data-ccp-props="{&quot;201341983&quot;:0,&quot;335559739&quot;:0,&quot;335559740&quot;:240}"> </span></p>
<hr />
<p><strong>Read parts one and two of the discussion:</strong><br />
<a href="https://semiengineering.com/agentic-ai-success-relies-on-excellent-human-scaffolding/">Agentic AI Success Relies On Excellent Human Scaffolding<br />
</a>Before deploying agentic AI into a chip design, engineers must define the domain ontology and agentic harness. Fundamental engines are still crucial.</p>
<p><a href="https://semiengineering.com/token-costs-are-becoming-the-new-eda-budget-battle/">Token Costs Are Becoming The New EDA Budget Battle<br />
</a>Cost per token is causing EDA design budgets to balloon; what comes next isn’t entirely clear yet.</p>

		<title>Building A Connected, Contextual Data Backbone For AI-Driven Semiconductor Design</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/building-a-connected-contextual-data-backbone-for-ai-driven-semiconductor-design/</link>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Why design teams must organize before they optimize and how to utilize a purpose-built foundation for AI-ready data management across the chip design lifecycle. </p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/building-a-connected-contextual-data-backbone-for-ai-driven-semiconductor-design/">Building A Connected, Contextual Data Backbone For AI-Driven Semiconductor Design</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Artificial Intelligence (AI) is redefining what’s possible in semiconductor design. From intelligent layout generation to predictive verification and generative IP reuse, AI promises to transform Electronic Design Automation (EDA) workflows and accelerate innovation. Yet despite the growing potential, most design environments are not ready to harness AI effectively.</p>
<p>The obstacle isn’t a lack of models or computational power—it’s the data.</p>
<p>AI-enhanced EDA workflows depend on structured, contextualized, and verifiable data. Without it, AI cannot learn efficiently, scale effectively, or deliver trustworthy insights. Fragmented repositories, inconsistent metadata, and undocumented IP reuse all obscure the relationships that give design data meaning. When data lacks organization and traceability, AI-driven automation becomes unreliable and difficult to implement.</p>
<p>The path to AI-driven design innovation begins with data organization, not algorithm selection. Before optimizing processes, semiconductor teams must first establish a strong, structured data foundation that connects every stage of the design lifecycle.</p>
<p>This white paper explores why organizing data is the first and most critical step toward AI readiness—and how Keysight SOS provides the purpose-built infrastructure to achieve it.</p>
<p>Read <a href="https://www.keysight.com/gb/en/assets/3125-1450/white-papers/Organize-Before-You-Optimize-The-AI-Ready-Data-Foundation.pdf">more here</a>.</p>
<p>&nbsp;</p>
<p>&nbsp;</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/building-a-connected-contextual-data-backbone-for-ai-driven-semiconductor-design/">Building A Connected, Contextual Data Backbone For AI-Driven Semiconductor Design</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>

		<title>Make Your Interface Work For Your AI  SoC—A 10 Step Program: Verification With Simulation</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/make-your-interface-work-for-your-ai-soc-a-10-step-program-verification-with-simulation/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/make-your-interface-work-for-your-ai-soc-a-10-step-program-verification-with-simulation/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Synopsys]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Wed, 23 Sep 2026 07:01:33 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[System-Level Design]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Whitepapers]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[AI in verification]]></category>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Best practices for reducing integration risk, shortening verification schedules, and improving productivity when deploying third-party interface IP in AI and heterogeneous SoC architectures.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/make-your-interface-work-for-your-ai-soc-a-10-step-program-verification-with-simulation/">Make Your Interface Work For Your AI  SoC—A 10 Step Program: Verification With Simulation</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>As AI SoCs integrate increasingly complex combinations of processors, accelerators, memory subsystems, and high-speed interfaces, verification challenges extend well beyond functional correctness. Modern designs must validate system integration, software interactions, interoperability, and performance across highly configurable third-party IP environments. This white paper explores how simulation-based verification helps engineering teams identify integration issues early and accelerate development cycles.</p>
<p>The paper examines the evolving role of Verification IP (VIP), Test Groups, and SoC Verification Kits (SVKs) in modern semiconductor verification flows. Readers will learn how these solutions provide protocol expertise, reusable verification content, and pre-integrated test environments that reduce integration risk, improve verification efficiency, and enable consistent validation from early RTL development through system-level verification.</p>
<p>What You Will Learn</p>
<ul>
<li>How Verification IP (VIP) helps validate integration correctness, software interactions, interoperability, and system-level KPIs for complex interface-based designs.</li>
</ul>
<ul>
<li>Why Test Groups provide a more scalable, use case-driven approach to interface verification than traditional monolithic test suites.</li>
</ul>
<ul>
<li>How SoC Verification Kits (SVKs) accelerate subsystem and SoC verification with pre-integrated environments, reusable verification assets, and proven methodologies.</li>
</ul>
<ul>
<li>Best practices for reducing integration risk, shortening verification schedules, and improving productivity when deploying third-party interface IP in AI and heterogeneous SoC architectures.</li>
</ul>
<p>Read <a href="https://www.synopsys.com/resources/make-your-interface-work-10-step-program-verification-with-simulation.html">more here</a>.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/make-your-interface-work-for-your-ai-soc-a-10-step-program-verification-with-simulation/">Make Your Interface Work For Your AI  SoC—A 10 Step Program: Verification With Simulation</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Digital twins and thermal sensors; agentic AI workflows; physical AI needs new silicon; RF design changes.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/blog-review-sept-23-3/">Blog Review: Sept. 23</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Siemens&#8217; Matteo Depaola and Robin Bornoff examine how physics-based digital twins for electronics can enable a handful of carefully placed physical <a href="https://blogs.sw.siemens.com/art-of-the-possible/towards-robust-optimal-sensor-placement-for-thermal-digital-twins-in-electronics/">thermal sensors</a> to provide the measurements needed to support many more virtual sensors throughout the system.</p>
<p>Synopsys&#8217; Thomas Andersen explores how <a href="https://www.synopsys.com/blogs/chip-design/agentic-ai-autonomous-engineering.html">agentic AI</a> systems change the unit of work from an individual prompt, command, or recommendation to a goal-directed workflow.</p>
<p>Cadence&#8217;s Max Zarco argues that traditional edge silicon can&#8217;t keep up with the demands of <a href="https://community.cadence.com/cadence_blogs_8/b/ip/posts/what-is-physical-ai-why-it-demands-a-new-class-of-silicon">physical AI</a>, which require multimodal workloads, stricter real-time constraints, and security anchored in hardware.</p>
<p>Keysight&#8217;s Richard Duvall finds that AI is fundamentally changing <a href="https://www.keysight.com/blogs/en/tech/sim-des/ai-driven-rf-design-from-scripts-to-autonomous-agents">RF design</a> by using advanced statistical models, deep learning networks, and automated reasoning to explore vast, high-dimensional RF design spaces rapidly.</p>
<p>Arm&#8217;s Julie Gaskin shares how <a href="https://developer.arm.com/community/arm-community-blogs/b/mobile-graphics-and-gaming-blog/posts/profile-neural-graphics-workloads-with-arm-streamline">neural workload profiling</a> can help developers identify latency, expensive graph operations, and shader fallbacks in applications that use the ML extensions for Vulkan.</p>
<p>The ESD Alliance&#8217;s Julie Rogers and Paul Cohen chat with Jay Vleeschhouwer of Griffin Securities about whether <a href="https://www.semi.org/en/blogs/inside-the-eda-growth-story-and-ai-impact-a-chat-with-jay-vleeschhouwer-of-griffin-securities">EDA growth</a> is sustainable, the impact of AI, 2027 revenue predictions.</p>
<p>Plus, check out the blogs featured in the latest <a href="https://semiengineering.com/newsletter/manufacturing-packaging-materials-sept-2026/">Manufacturing, Packaging &amp; Materials newsletter</a>:</p>
<p>Mitsubishi Chemical Group’s Hideaki Okamoto looks at why expanding computational capabilities and deeper co-development are changing how <a href="https://semiengineering.com/beyond-scaling-the-growing-role-of-materials-innovation-in-semiconductor-manufacturing/">materials are moving</a> from lab to fab.</p>
<p>Amkor’s Chiung Lee outlines how thinner dies, taller stacks, and hybrid bonding are carrying <a href="https://semiengineering.com/ais-storage-problem-is-a-packaging-problem/">NAND into the AI era</a>, driven by data growth across consumer electronics, automotive, enterprise, and cloud.</p>
<p>Lam Research’s Swapnil Kailash More illustrates how small imbalances between <a href="https://semiengineering.com/virtual-fabrication-meets-stress-physics-solving-gaa-channel-non-uniformity/">stacked nanosheets</a> can distort device behavior in ways that are difficult to predict from geometry alone.</p>
<p>Intel Foundry’s Lalitha Immaneni contends that <a href="https://semiengineering.com/from-silicon-to-systems-heterogeneous-integration-as-the-engine-of-ai-performance/">design space exploration</a> must become a core capability for advanced packaging and chiplet-based systems.</p>
<p>Synopsys’ Larry Melvin discusses wafer-validated <a href="https://semiengineering.com/predicting-silicon-behavior-years-before-test-wafers/">optical simulation</a> for high-NA EUV applications, enabled by early lithography pathfinding, process optimization, and analysis.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/blog-review-sept-23-3/">Blog Review: Sept. 23</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Researchers at Carnegie Mellon University, University of Florida, MIT, Texas A&#38;M University et al. published a technical paper titled “Wafer-scale 2D MoS₂ transistors with sub-5 nm channel length and subthreshold performance beyond the silicon limit.” Abstract Excerpt “Here, we report monolayer MoS₂ transistors with physical channel lengths below 5 nm, achieving a subthreshold swing of 88 mV/dec... <a class="read_more" href="https://semiengineering.com/wafer-scale-sub-5nm-channel-monolayer-mos2-transistors-cmu-uf-mit-et-al/">&#187; read more</a></p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Researchers at <strong>Carnegie Mellon University, University of Florida, MIT, Texas A&amp;M University </strong>et al. published a technical paper titled “Wafer-scale 2D MoS₂ transistors with sub-5 nm channel length and subthreshold performance beyond the silicon limit.”</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph"><strong>Abstract Excerpt</strong></p>
<p>“Here, we report monolayer MoS₂ transistors with physical channel lengths below 5 nm, achieving a subthreshold swing of 88 mV/dec and an on/off ratio above 10<sup>6</sup>. These results surpass both the theoretical subthreshold limit of silicon and state-of-the-art emerging semiconductors-based transistors at comparable dimensions. To ensure high throughput, we develop a photolithography based, complementary metal oxide semiconductor (CMOS) compatible process and demonstrate 4-inch wafer-scale integration.”</p>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Researchers at the University of Toronto published a technical paper titled “GPUThor: Amplifying Rowhammer Attacks via Non-Uniform Patterns to Exploit ECC-Protected GPUs.” Abstract Excerpt “We present GPUThor, a high-intensity Rowhammer attack on NVIDIA GPUs leveraging non-uniform hammering. GPUThor reverse engineers GPU memory-access coalescing behavior to enable non-uniform hammering patterns on GPUs, that activate aggressor rows... <a class="read_more" href="https://semiengineering.com/high-intensity-rowhammer-attack-on-gpus-leveraging-non-uniform-hammering-u-of-toronto/">&#187; read more</a></p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/high-intensity-rowhammer-attack-on-gpus-leveraging-non-uniform-hammering-u-of-toronto/">High-Intensity Rowhammer Attack On GPUs Leveraging Non-uniform Hammering (U. of Toronto)</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Researchers at the <strong>University of Toronto</strong> published a technical paper titled “GPUThor: Amplifying Rowhammer Attacks via Non-Uniform Patterns to Exploit ECC-Protected GPUs.”</p>
<p><strong>Abstract Excerpt</strong></p>
<p>“We present GPUThor, a high-intensity Rowhammer attack on NVIDIA GPUs leveraging non-uniform hammering. GPUThor reverse engineers GPU memory-access coalescing behavior to enable non-uniform hammering patterns on GPUs, that activate aggressor rows more intensely than decoy rows. Additionally, by identifying refresh instances when in-DRAM mitigations are applied, it constructs longer attack patterns that escape mitigation across refresh intervals, further increasing hammering intensity. ”</p>
<p>Find the <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.16546v1">technical paper here.</a> September 2026.</p>
<p>Lin, Chris S., Joyce Qu, Aditya Rajeev, and Gururaj Saileshwar. &#8220;GPUThor: Amplifying Rowhammer Attacks via Non-Uniform Patterns to Exploit ECC-Protected GPUs.&#8221; arXiv preprint arXiv:2609.16546 (2026).</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/high-intensity-rowhammer-attack-on-gpus-leveraging-non-uniform-hammering-u-of-toronto/">High-Intensity Rowhammer Attack On GPUs Leveraging Non-uniform Hammering (U. of Toronto)</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>

		<item>
		<title>From Test Compression To Hierarchical Connectivity: Scaling SoC Test For AI And HPC Devices</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/from-test-compression-to-hierarchical-connectivity-scaling-soc-test-for-ai-and-hpc-devices/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/from-test-compression-to-hierarchical-connectivity-scaling-soc-test-for-ai-and-hpc-devices/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Sri Ganta]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Tue, 22 Sep 2026 07:01:51 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Blogs - PTES]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Silicon Lifecycle Management]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Test, Measurement and Analytics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[AI]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[design for test]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[DFT]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[HPC]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[scan test]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[streaming network]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Synopsys]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[test]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[test compression]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[test data]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://semiengineering.com/?p=24281787</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>While compression reduces test data volume, efficient distribution of test data remains equally important. </p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/from-test-compression-to-hierarchical-connectivity-scaling-soc-test-for-ai-and-hpc-devices/">From Test Compression To Hierarchical Connectivity: Scaling SoC Test For AI And HPC Devices</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Modern AI and HPC devices are challenging traditional test architectures. As scan data volume, core counts, chiplet integration, and test coverage requirements continue to increase, conventional DFT methodologies are becoming difficult to scale. Synopsys TestMAX Unified Compression, based on DFTMAX SEQ, and Streaming Fabric (SF), a programmable high-bandwidth test data delivery network, provide a new approach that enables scalable, hierarchical, and efficient testing for the next generation of AI compute systems.</p>
<h2>The growing test challenge for AI and HPC designs</h2>
<p>AI accelerators and HPC processors are fundamentally different from traditional SoCs.</p>
<p>Today&#8217;s devices may contain:</p>
<ul>
<li>Hundreds of millions of scan flip-flops</li>
<li>Hundreds or thousands of replicated IP blocks</li>
<li>Large tile-based architecture</li>
<li>Multi-die and chiplet configurations</li>
<li>Extremely aggressive test coverage goals</li>
</ul>
<p>These factors are driving exponential growth in test data volume (TDV), routing complexity, tester bandwidth requirements, diagnosis challenges, and overall test cost. Traditional flat scan architectures often struggle with limited test pins, congestion caused by large scan buses, uneven bandwidth allocation, and inefficient utilization of available test resources.</p>
<h2>Why traditional DFT methodologies reach their limits</h2>
<p>Conventional gate-level DFT methodologies were developed for an earlier generation of SoCs. As designs grow larger, several challenges emerge:</p>
<ul>
<li>Thousands of parallel scan chains create routing congestion</li>
<li>Test pin planning becomes constrained by limited package resources</li>
<li>Timing closure is disrupted by test infrastructure</li>
<li>Verification issues are often discovered late in the design cycle</li>
<li>Large number of clock and power domains increases test data volumes beyond tester memory limits</li>
<li>Design updates create expensive front-end and back-end rework loops</li>
</ul>
<h2>Unified compression: One architecture across the silicon lifecycle</h2>
<p>A critical requirement for modern AI chips is the ability to reuse test infrastructure across manufacturing, burn-in, system-level test, and in-field test environments.</p>
<p>Synopsys Unified Compression Architecture addresses this requirement through a comprehensive sequential compression architecture that provides:</p>
<ul>
<li>Re-seedable PRPG-based test pattern generation</li>
<li>MISR-based response compaction</li>
<li>High data compression ratios</li>
<li>Low pin-count implementation</li>
<li>Built-in diagnostic capabilities</li>
<li>Support for IEEE 1687 infrastructure</li>
<li>Support for X-tolerant LBIST and in-system testing environments</li>
</ul>
<p>Rather than deploying different compression hardware for each phase of the silicon lifecycle, a unified codec can be reused across multiple test modes and environments. This reduces implementation complexity while improving test coverage and diagnosis.</p>
<p>Additional benefits include:</p>
<ul>
<li>Reduced test data volume</li>
<li>Lower tester memory requirements</li>
<li>Improved diagnosis efficiency</li>
<li>Reduced DFT area overhead</li>
<li>Configurable power-management capabilities during testing</li>
</ul>
<h2>Streaming fabric: The missing link for large-scale AI SoCs</h2>
<p>While compression reduces test data volume, efficient distribution of test data remains equally important. This is where Streaming Fabric (SF) becomes transformative.</p>
<p>Streaming Fabric acts as a programmable high-bandwidth data-delivery infrastructure capable of efficiently transporting compressed test data across large hierarchical designs. Instead of relying on thousands of dedicated scan routes, scan traffic is packetized and transported through a configurable streaming network.</p>
<p>Key capabilities include:</p>
<ul>
<li>Dynamic bandwidth management</li>
<li>Broadcast delivery to replicated cores</li>
<li>Configurable routing paths</li>
<li>Multi-branch parallel execution</li>
<li>Hierarchical scalability</li>
<li>Support for GPIO and HSIO-based access</li>
<li>IEEE 1838 compatibility for multi-die package architectures</li>
</ul>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24281788" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Synopsys_Test-Compression-Hierarchical-Connectivity-fig1.webp?resize=744%2C611&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="744" height="611" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Synopsys_Test-Compression-Hierarchical-Connectivity-fig1.webp?w=744&amp;ssl=1 744w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Synopsys_Test-Compression-Hierarchical-Connectivity-fig1.webp?resize=300%2C246&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Synopsys_Test-Compression-Hierarchical-Connectivity-fig1.webp?resize=600%2C493&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="(max-width: 744px) 100vw, 744px" /></p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24281789" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Synopsys_Test-Compression-Hierarchical-Connectivity-fig2.webp?resize=791%2C207&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="791" height="207" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Synopsys_Test-Compression-Hierarchical-Connectivity-fig2.webp?w=791&amp;ssl=1 791w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Synopsys_Test-Compression-Hierarchical-Connectivity-fig2.webp?resize=300%2C79&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Synopsys_Test-Compression-Hierarchical-Connectivity-fig2.webp?resize=768%2C201&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Synopsys_Test-Compression-Hierarchical-Connectivity-fig2.webp?resize=600%2C157&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 791px) 100vw, 791px" /></p>
<h2>Enabling a shift-left test methodology</h2>
<p>One of the most important innovations is the move toward test architecture development at RTL.</p>
<p>Using TestMAX Manager, designers can:</p>
<ol>
<li>Create RTL for DFT IP based on user specifications</li>
<li>Read functional RTL and integrate DFT IP and network</li>
<li>Validate and extract DFT structures for test readiness</li>
<li>Visualize DFT network and interactively debug any violations</li>
<li>Generate simulation testbenches and constraints for implementation flows</li>
</ol>
<p>This approach enables earlier verification, earlier DRC closure, and improved consistency between RTL and implementation databases. The result is a &#8220;correct-by-construction&#8221; methodology that significantly reduces expensive re-design iterations later in the project.</p>
<h2>A foundation for the future of AI test</h2>
<p>The combination of Unified Compression and Streaming Fabric represents more than an incremental improvement in DFT technology. Together, these technologies create a scalable infrastructure that addresses the test challenges introduced by AI-scale designs:</p>
<ul>
<li>Massive scan data volume</li>
<li>Hierarchical architectures</li>
<li>Replicated IP structures</li>
<li>Chiplets and heterogeneous integration</li>
<li>In-system and in-field testing requirements</li>
<li>Aggressive quality targets and low DPPM goals</li>
</ul>
<p>Unified Compression and Streaming Fabric (SF) provide a practical implementation methodology capable of scaling from individual IP blocks to large AI accelerators containing hundreds of millions of scan elements while simplifying integration, reducing physical design complexity, and improving overall test efficiency.</p>
<p>As AI systems continue to grow in scale and complexity, <a href="https://www.synopsys.com/implementation-and-signoff/test-automation.html">Synopsys TestMAX and STAR Memory System (SMS) IP family</a> of products provide a robust foundation for delivering high-quality, cost-effective, and scalable test solutions throughout the silicon lifecycle.</p>
<h3>References</h3>
<p><strong>Synopsys Silicon to Systems Blog: </strong><a href="https://www.synopsys.com/blogs/chip-design/ai-hpc-chip-test-solutions-seq-compression-streaming-fabric.html">Addressing AI and HPC Chip Test Challenges with TestMAX SEQ Compression and Streaming Fabric</a>; by <a href="https://www.synopsys.com/authors/jon-colburn.html">Jon Colburn</a>, <a href="https://www.synopsys.com/authors/sri-ganta.html">Sri Ganta</a>, Synopsys</p>
